title: Async & Concurrency for Agents
summary: Agents spend most of their time waiting on I/O — model calls and tool calls that take seconds. Running them one at a time wastes that wait; asyncio lets a single thread issue many calls concurrently and interleave them while each awaits its response. You launch many coroutines, gather their results, and bound how many run at once with a semaphore so you don't blow past provider rate limits or exhaust memory. The one rule that makes it all work: never block the event loop with synchronous CPU or blocking I/O.

subtopics.title: Async fits I/O-bound agent work
subtopics.explanation: A model call or a tool HTTP request spends nearly all its time waiting on the network, not using the CPU. Running ten such calls sequentially takes the sum of their latencies, but issuing them concurrently takes about the latency of the slowest one, because while each awaits its response the event loop runs the others. This I/O-bound profile is exactly what asyncio is built for, which is why it is the default concurrency model for agents.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio, time

async def fake_model_call(name: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(1)          # simulate ~1s of network wait
    return f"{name} done"

async def main() -> None:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    # ten calls run concurrently -> ~1s total, not ~10s
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fake_model_call(f"c{i}") for i in range(10)))
    print(len(results), "calls in", round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1), "s")

asyncio.run(main())   # prints: 10 calls in ~1.0 s

subtopics.title: Coroutines, await, and the event loop
subtopics.explanation: An async def function is a coroutine; calling it returns a coroutine object that does nothing until awaited or scheduled. await yields control back to the event loop while an operation is pending, letting the loop run other ready coroutines in the meantime. Understanding that await is a cooperative yield point — not a background thread — is what lets you reason about when your code makes progress and when it hands off.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio

async def step(n: int) -> int:
    print(f"start {n}")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)   # yield to the loop; other coroutines run here
    print(f"end {n}")
    return n * 2

async def main() -> None:
    # scheduling both means their prints interleave around the await
    a, b = await asyncio.gather(step(1), step(2))
    print("results", a, b)

asyncio.run(main())

subtopics.title: Gather many results at once
subtopics.explanation: asyncio.gather schedules a batch of coroutines together and returns their results in the same order you passed them, awaiting until all complete. With return_exceptions=True a failure in one coroutine is returned as a value instead of cancelling the whole batch, so a single bad tool call doesn't take down the rest. Gathering is the primary way an agent fans out to many tools or sub-tasks and collects their answers.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio

async def tool_call(i: int) -> str:
    if i == 2:
        raise RuntimeError("tool 2 failed")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return f"result {i}"

async def main() -> None:
    # return_exceptions keeps one failure from cancelling the others
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        *(tool_call(i) for i in range(4)),
        return_exceptions=True,
    )
    for r in results:
        print("ERR" if isinstance(r, Exception) else "OK", r)

asyncio.run(main())

subtopics.title: Bound concurrency with a semaphore
subtopics.explanation: Unbounded fan-out can launch thousands of calls at once, instantly tripping provider rate limits and exhausting memory or file descriptors. An asyncio.Semaphore caps how many coroutines run the protected section simultaneously — each acquires a slot before calling and releases it after — so you get concurrency without a stampede. Bounding concurrency is what lets an agent go fast while staying inside quota and resource limits.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)   # at most 5 in flight at once

async def limited_call(i: int) -> str:
    async with sem:                       # acquire a slot; auto-release on exit
        await asyncio.sleep(0.2)          # the real model/tool call
        return f"done {i}"

async def main() -> None:
    # 100 tasks scheduled, but never more than 5 run concurrently
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(limited_call(i) for i in range(100)))
    print("completed", len(results), "with max concurrency 5")

asyncio.run(main())

subtopics.title: Never block the event loop
subtopics.explanation: The event loop runs on one thread, so any synchronous work that doesn't await — a CPU-heavy loop, a blocking requests.get, or time.sleep — freezes every other coroutine until it finishes. You offload blocking or CPU-bound work to a thread or process pool via asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor so the loop stays free to progress other tasks. Keeping the loop unblocked is the single discipline that separates concurrency that works from code that mysteriously stalls.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio, time

def blocking_parse(data: str) -> int:
    time.sleep(0.5)          # simulate a blocking/CPU-bound library
    return len(data)

async def handle(data: str) -> int:
    # offload the blocking call so the loop keeps serving other coroutines
    return await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_parse, data)

async def main() -> None:
    # both run concurrently because neither blocks the loop
    a, b = await asyncio.gather(handle("xxxx"), handle("yy"))
    print(a, b)

asyncio.run(main())

foundations.overview: Agents are I/O-bound: they spend seconds per step waiting on model and tool calls rather than burning CPU. Running those calls sequentially wastes almost all of that time idling. asyncio lets a single thread hold many in-flight calls at once — while each awaits its network response, the event loop advances the others — so a batch of N calls finishes in roughly the time of the slowest instead of the sum of all. You create coroutines with async def, await them at cooperative yield points, and collect a fan-out with asyncio.gather (using return_exceptions=True so one failure doesn't cancel the batch). Because unbounded fan-out would instantly trip provider rate limits and exhaust resources, you cap parallelism with an asyncio.Semaphore. And because the loop is single-threaded, the cardinal rule is to never block it: offload any CPU-bound or blocking-I/O work to a thread or process pool via asyncio.to_thread. Get these right and one process can drive hundreds of concurrent agent and tool calls efficiently.
foundations.formalDefinition: asyncio concurrency for agents is cooperative multitasking on a single-threaded event loop: coroutines (async def functions) run until they await, yielding control so other ready coroutines progress; asyncio.gather schedules and joins a batch of coroutines; an asyncio.Semaphore bounds the number concurrently executing a critical section; and blocking or CPU-bound work must be offloaded (asyncio.to_thread / run_in_executor) so the loop is never blocked.
foundations.whyItMatters: The throughput and cost of an agent service are dominated by how well it overlaps waiting. Sequential calls make a multi-tool step take seconds times the tool count and cap how many users one worker can serve. Concurrency collapses that wall-clock time and multiplies per-worker throughput, while bounded concurrency keeps you inside provider quotas — together they are what make an agent service both fast and affordable.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of one skilled chef (the single thread) cooking many dishes. Sequential cooking is starting one dish, standing at the oven until it's done, then starting the next. Async is putting a dish in the oven (await) and, while it bakes, prepping the next — the chef is never idle while something cooks. The semaphore is having only five oven racks, so no matter how many orders arrive, at most five bake at once. Blocking the loop is the chef stopping to hand-whisk for ten minutes, during which nothing else in any oven gets checked.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Fanning out a research agent's queries to many sources at once, running independent tool calls in a single agent step concurrently, processing a batch of documents through an extraction agent in parallel, and serving many user sessions from one async worker without a thread per request.
foundations.performanceImpact: Concurrency turns N sequential I/O-bound calls (sum of latencies) into roughly the latency of the slowest, and lets one process serve far more sessions than a thread-per-request model. The semaphore caps peak load to stay under quota, and offloading blocking work prevents a single stall from freezing all in-flight tasks — protecting p99 latency.
commonUseCases: Fanning out research/search queries to many sources concurrently
Running independent tool calls in one agent step in parallel
Batch-processing documents through an agent in parallel
Serving many user sessions from one async worker

commonMisconceptions.myth: asyncio makes code run on multiple CPU cores.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The event loop is single-threaded; asyncio overlaps waiting, not computation. CPU-bound work needs a process pool — asyncio only speeds up I/O-bound concurrency.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Calling an async function runs it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Calling a coroutine returns a coroutine object that does nothing until you await it or schedule it (e.g. via gather/create_task). Forgetting to await is a common silent bug.
Unbounded fan-out trips rate limits, exhausts file descriptors and memory, and can slow everything down. A semaphore-bounded pool is usually faster and far safer than launching everything at once.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A blocking call inside a coroutine is fine.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A synchronous blocking call (requests.get, time.sleep, heavy CPU) freezes the whole event loop, stalling every other coroutine. Offload it with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.

interactiveExamples.title: Sequential vs concurrent fan-out
interactiveExamples.explanation: Run the same set of simulated calls first one at a time, then concurrently with gather, and compare the wall-clock time. The concurrent version finishes in about the slowest call's duration instead of the sum.

code.code:
import asyncio, time

async def call(name: str, delay: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return name

async def sequential(jobs):
    return [await call(n, d) for n, d in jobs]

async def concurrent(jobs):
    return await asyncio.gather(*(call(n, d) for n, d in jobs))

async def main() -> None:
    jobs = [("a", 0.3), ("b", 0.3), ("c", 0.3)]
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await sequential(jobs)
    seq = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await concurrent(jobs)
    con = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"sequential ~{round(seq, 1)}s  concurrent ~{round(con, 1)}s")

asyncio.run(main())
code.caption: Three 0.3s calls take ~0.9s sequentially but ~0.3s concurrently, because the waits overlap on the event loop.

interactiveExamples.title: Bounded concurrency with a semaphore
interactiveExamples.explanation: Fan out many tasks but cap how many run at once with a semaphore, tracking the peak concurrency actually reached. Even with far more tasks than slots, the peak never exceeds the limit.

code.code:
import asyncio

async def worker(i, sem, state):
    async with sem:
        state["live"] += 1
        state["peak"] = max(state["peak"], state["live"])
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)   # the real call would go here
        state["live"] -= 1
        return i

async def main() -> None:
    limit = 4
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)
    state = {"live": 0, "peak": 0}
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        *(worker(i, sem, state) for i in range(20))
    )
    print("tasks completed:", len(results))
    print("limit:", limit, "peak concurrency:", state["peak"])
    print("peak within limit:", state["peak"] <= limit)

asyncio.run(main())
code.caption: Twenty tasks share four slots; the measured peak concurrency never exceeds the semaphore's limit.
code.expectedOutput:
tasks completed: 20
limit: 4 peak concurrency: 4
peak within limit: True

codeLab.title: Build a bounded concurrent map
codeLab.instructions: Implement async def bounded_gather(coros, limit) that runs an iterable of coroutines with at most `limit` running concurrently, returns their results in the SAME order as the input, and — like asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True) — returns any raised exception as its result value instead of cancelling the batch. Use an asyncio.Semaphore to bound concurrency. Do not let one coroutine's failure stop the others. Complete the function so the harness passes.

starter.code:
import asyncio

async def bounded_gather(coros, limit):
    # TODO: run coros with at most `limit` concurrent, preserve input order,
    # and capture exceptions as result values (do not cancel the batch).
    ...

solution.code:
import asyncio

async def bounded_gather(coros, limit):
    coros = list(coros)
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)

    async def run(coro):
        async with sem:                 # acquire a slot before awaiting
            try:
                return await coro
            except Exception as e:       # capture, don't propagate
                return e

    # gather preserves order; return_exceptions is unneeded since run() never raises
    return await asyncio.gather(*(run(c) for c in coros))

codeLab.testHarness:
import asyncio

async def ok(i, live, peak):
    live[0] += 1
    peak[0] = max(peak[0], live[0])
    await asyncio.sleep(0.02)
    live[0] -= 1
    return i * 10

async def boom(i):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    raise ValueError(f"fail {i}")

async def main():
    live, peak = [0], [0]
    coros = []
    for i in range(10):
        coros.append(boom(i) if i == 3 else ok(i, live, peak))
    results = await bounded_gather(coros, limit=3)

    # order preserved
    assert results[0] == 0 and results[1] == 10 and results[9] == 90, results
    # the failing coroutine's exception is captured, not raised
    assert isinstance(results[3], ValueError), results[3]
    # concurrency never exceeded the limit
    assert peak[0] <= 3, peak[0]
    print("all tests passed")

asyncio.run(main())
hints: Wrap each coroutine in an inner async helper that does `async with sem:` then `await coro`.
Catch Exception inside the helper and return it, so the helper itself never raises and can't cancel the gather.
asyncio.gather already returns results in the order the coroutines were passed, so build the helper list in input order.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does asyncio speed up an agent making many model calls but NOT a CPU-heavy computation?
options: asyncio uses multiple CPU cores for both
asyncio overlaps I/O waiting on one thread; CPU work doesn't await, so it can't interleave
CPU work is always faster than I/O
asyncio only works with the network
checkpoints.explanation: The event loop is single-threaded and only makes progress on other coroutines when one awaits. I/O-bound calls await while waiting, so they overlap; a CPU-bound loop never awaits, so it blocks the loop and gains nothing — use a process pool for that.

checkpoints.prompt: This coroutine tanks the whole agent's concurrency. Why?
checkpoints.code:
import requests, time
async def fetch(url):
    time.sleep(0.5)              # 'rate limit' pause
    return requests.get(url).text
options: time.sleep and requests.get are synchronous and block the single-threaded event loop, freezing every other coroutine
checkpoints.explanation: Both time.sleep and requests.get are blocking synchronous calls. On the single-threaded loop they freeze all other coroutines. Use await asyncio.sleep and an async HTTP client (or asyncio.to_thread for the blocking call).

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print, and why doesn't the batch crash?
checkpoints.code:
import asyncio
async def f(i):
    if i == 1: raise ValueError("x")
    return i
async def main():
    r = await asyncio.gather(f(0), f(1), f(2), return_exceptions=True)
    print([type(x).__name__ for x in r])
asyncio.run(main())
options: It raises ValueError and prints nothing
checkpoints.explanation: With return_exceptions=True, gather returns the raised ValueError as a result value (in order) instead of propagating it, so the batch completes. f(0) and f(2) return ints; f(1)'s slot holds the ValueError.

theory.question: Explain why asyncio is the right concurrency model for an agent and where it stops helping.
theory.directAnswer: Agents are I/O-bound — they mostly wait on model and tool calls — and asyncio overlaps that waiting on a single thread, so many calls finish in about the time of the slowest instead of the sum, with far less overhead than a thread per request. It stops helping for CPU-bound work: the event loop is single-threaded, so heavy computation blocks it and must be offloaded to a process pool.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Cooperative single-threaded concurrency where coroutines yield at await points, letting the event loop interleave many in-flight I/O operations.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Thread-per-request scales poorly for thousands of mostly-idle connections; an event loop overlaps waiting cheaply without per-request thread overhead or heavy locking.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Coroutines run until they await an I/O operation, yielding to the loop, which resumes them when their result is ready; gather fans out and joins, and a semaphore bounds how many run at once.

theory.whyImportant: It's the foundation of a high-throughput agent worker — it decides how many concurrent sessions and tool calls one process can serve and at what latency.
theory.realWorldExample: A research agent issuing 12 source queries per step dropped step latency from ~6s (sequential) to ~0.7s by gathering the queries concurrently under a semaphore.

followUps.question: How would you run a CPU-bound tool without blocking?
followUps.answer: Offload it with loop.run_in_executor using a ProcessPoolExecutor (or asyncio.to_thread for GIL-releasing/blocking-I/O work), so the event loop keeps serving other coroutines.

followUps.question: What's the cost of using async everywhere?
followUps.answer: It's viral — everything in the call path must be async or offloaded, libraries must be async-compatible, and a single accidental blocking call can stall the whole loop, so it demands discipline.

theory.question: Why bound concurrency with a semaphore instead of just launching every coroutine at once?
theory.directAnswer: Unbounded fan-out schedules everything simultaneously, which instantly trips provider rate limits, can exhaust file descriptors, sockets, and memory, and often makes the whole batch slower or fail. A semaphore caps how many run at once, giving you concurrency's speedup while staying inside quota and resource limits.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: asyncio.Semaphore(limit) is a counter that coroutines acquire before a critical section and release after, blocking additional acquirers once the limit is reached.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real dependencies have finite capacity (rate limits, connection pools); launching thousands of calls at once overwhelms them and yourself, causing 429s and resource exhaustion.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each coroutine does `async with sem:` around its call; only `limit` are ever inside at once, and as each finishes it releases a slot for a queued coroutine.

theory.whyImportant: It's the throttle that lets an agent go fast without stampeding a provider or crashing the worker — the practical bridge between concurrency and rate limits.
theory.realWorldExample: A batch job launched 5,000 extraction coroutines at once and got mass-429'd; wrapping them in a Semaphore(20) kept it under quota and actually finished sooner because nothing was being throttled.

followUps.question: How do you pick the limit?
followUps.answer: Base it on the provider's rate/concurrency quota and your connection-pool size, leaving headroom; tune empirically by watching 429 rate and throughput.

followUps.question: How does this relate to a shared fleet-wide limit?
followUps.answer: A per-process semaphore isn't enough when many workers share one quota; you also need a shared/distributed limiter (e.g. token bucket in Redis) so the aggregate stays under quota.

scenario.question: After moving your agent worker to asyncio, throughput barely improved and latency got spiky. How do you find and fix the problem?
scenario.directAnswer: The usual cause is a blocking call inside a coroutine — a synchronous HTTP client, time.sleep, JSON parsing of huge payloads, or a CPU-bound tool — that freezes the single-threaded loop. Detect it with asyncio's debug mode / slow-callback warnings, then make every I/O call truly async and offload CPU/blocking work with asyncio.to_thread or a process pool. Also verify you're actually awaiting concurrently (gather/create_task), not awaiting each call in sequence.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A diagnosis of lost concurrency, where code is 'async' in name but still runs effectively sequentially or stalls the loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Mixing a synchronous library (requests, a blocking DB driver, heavy CPU) into a coroutine blocks the loop; and `await`-ing calls one after another instead of gathering them keeps them serial.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Enable PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG / loop.slow_callback_duration to surface long-running callbacks, replace blocking clients with async ones (or wrap in to_thread), and restructure sequential awaits into gather/create_task so waits overlap.

scenario.whyImportant: It captures the most common asyncio failure in agent code and the disciplined way to isolate it, rather than assuming async automatically means fast.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team's async worker was still using requests inside coroutines; every call blocked the loop so nothing overlapped. Switching to an async HTTP client and gathering the calls cut p99 latency by 5x.

followUps.question: How do you catch a blocking call in tests?
followUps.answer: Run with debug mode enabled and set a low slow_callback_duration so any callback that hogs the loop logs a warning you can fail CI on.

followUps.question: Why can awaiting in a loop still be sequential?
followUps.answer: `for c in coros: await c` runs each to completion before starting the next; you must schedule them together (gather/create_task) for the waits to overlap.

coding.question: Write an async function that runs a list of async tool calls with bounded concurrency and a per-call timeout, returning results in order with timeouts/failures captured as error markers rather than crashing the batch.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need three things: a semaphore to bound concurrency, asyncio.wait_for to enforce a per-call timeout, and per-call exception capture so one failure or timeout doesn't sink the batch. I wrap each coroutine in a helper that acquires the semaphore, applies the timeout, and returns either the result or a tagged error tuple. gather preserves input order, so the returned list lines up with the inputs.

solution.code:
import asyncio

async def run_tools(coros, limit=5, timeout=10.0):
    coros = list(coros)
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)

    async def guarded(coro):
        async with sem:                          # bound concurrency
            try:
                return ("ok", await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout))
            except asyncio.TimeoutError:
                return ("timeout", None)
            except Exception as e:                # capture any other failure
                return ("error", repr(e))

    # gather preserves order; guarded never raises, so the batch never crashes
    return await asyncio.gather(*(guarded(c) for c in coros))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    async def quick(i):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return i
    async def slow():
        await asyncio.sleep(5)     # will hit the timeout
        return "never"
    async def bad():
        raise ValueError("boom")

    async def main():
        results = await run_tools([quick(1), slow(), bad()], limit=2, timeout=0.2)
        for r in results:
            print(r)

    asyncio.run(main())

lineByLine: We materialize the coroutines and create a Semaphore sized to the concurrency limit.
guarded acquires a semaphore slot with `async with sem:` so at most `limit` run at once.
asyncio.wait_for enforces a per-call timeout, raising asyncio.TimeoutError if the call runs too long.
A timeout returns a ('timeout', None) marker; any other exception returns ('error', repr(e)) — the helper never raises.
asyncio.gather runs all guarded wrappers and preserves input order in the returned list.
The __main__ demo shows a fast success, a call that times out, and a failing call all handled without crashing the batch.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) scheduling over n coroutines; wall-clock is bounded by ceil(n/limit) * per-call time (or the timeout).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the coroutine wrappers and the results list.

followUps.question: How would you add retries per call here?
followUps.answer: Wrap the `await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout)` in a bounded retry loop with async backoff (await asyncio.sleep), but note a coroutine can only be awaited once — retry by recreating it via a factory rather than reusing the object.

followUps.question: Why capture exceptions inside guarded instead of using gather(return_exceptions=True)?
followUps.answer: Doing it inside lets you distinguish timeouts from other errors and attach structured markers, giving richer, uniform results than gather's raw exception objects.

keyTakeaways: Agents are I/O-bound; asyncio overlaps the waiting on one thread so N concurrent calls take about the slowest one's latency, not the sum.
A coroutine does nothing until awaited or scheduled; use asyncio.gather (with return_exceptions=True) to fan out and collect results in order.
Bound fan-out with an asyncio.Semaphore so you get concurrency without tripping rate limits or exhausting sockets, memory, and file descriptors.
Never block the single-threaded event loop — offload CPU-bound or synchronous-blocking work with asyncio.to_thread or a process pool.
asyncio speeds up I/O concurrency, not computation; combine it with per-call timeouts and a shared limiter to stay fast and within quota.
